summary: The English is close to the Hebrew and the unit's one serious error is 19:36, where the definite 'the two daughters of Lot' became 'two daughters'. Several grammar notes are false (19:34 says the two proposals belong to different daughters, 19:35 says only the younger 'arose and lay' while the elder made drink), Ibn Ezra's point on בְּשִׁכְבָהּ and Rashi's on 19:33 and 19:36 are misreported, the literal lines print the preposition אֵת as an object marker, and the ketiv/qere of הִוא (19:38) and the meanings of Moab and Ben-ammi in the glosses are missing. The English 'keep alive seed' is replaced by 'preserve offspring'; some comments were unruled and context notes were added.

patches.value: Ramban: perhaps they reasoned that they should do what was fitting, that God would have mercy, and that a male and a female would be born and the world would continue through them ('the world is built by kindness', Ps 89:3), since the LORD had not saved them for nothing. They were modest and did not tell their father to take them, because a descendant of Noah may marry his daughter, or because the thing was very ugly in the eyes of those generations and had never been done; and our rabbis in the aggadot condemn Lot severely. This is the motive the daughters may have had; it is not a gloss on any word, so the English gives none.
patches.reason: The summary left out Ramban's explanation of why they used wine and did not ask their father, and his citation of the rabbis' censure of Lot.

value.summary: Radak: one who leaves no seed is as dead, if he leaves nothing after him by which his name is remembered. This gives the daughters' reason for wanting offspring; it does not bear on the wording of the English.

patches.reason: a comment on this verse that the translation did not rule on

value: In the world of the text a family line continues through children, above all sons, and the name of a dead man is kept alive by his descendants. To be left without offspring was to be cut off; many stories in Genesis turn on this. The daughters give exactly this aim: to preserve offspring from their father.
patches.reason: a reader needs the setting of the daughters' aim

patches.value: The article is on the noun (הַלַּיְלָה, with the ב: 'in the night'). The demonstrative הוּא 'that' follows without its own article, though the article is expected (הַהוּא, as in 19:35). Radak calls this the lack of the ה of the definite article on the adjective and compares 2 Sam 6:3 and Num 28:4.
patches.reason: The note said the demonstrative 'does the work of the adjective', which misses Radak's point: the demonstrative lacks the article.

patches.value: Infinitive construct with ב and a 3rd feminine singular suffix: 'in her lying down'. Ibn Ezra: it is the infinitive (שֵׁם הַפּוֹעַל), though its first vowel is hireq (שִׁכְבָהּ), as in בְּשִׁבְרִי לָכֶם (Lev 26:26). The plain 'lying down' is the act with her father in the context.
patches.reason: The note said the posture sense 'carries the euphemism', which says nothing; and Ibn Ezra's point is the hireq vowel of the first letter, not of the ב.

patches.value: Ibn Ezra: בְּשִׁכְבָהּ is the infinitive (שֵׁם הַפּוֹעַל), even though its first letter has a hireq, like בְּשִׁבְרִי לָכֶם (Lev 26:26). The English reads it as the event: 'when she lay down'.
patches.reason: The summary said the ב may carry the hireq; Ibn Ezra says the first radical has the hireq (שִׁכְ-), like שִׁבְרִי.

patches.value: Rashi: of the younger it is written 'and she lay with him' (not 'with her father'); because she did not begin the immorality but her sister taught her, scripture spared her and did not spell out her shame, whereas the firstborn, who began it, scripture exposes explicitly ('with her father'). A moral reading of the wording; the English renders both acts alike.
patches.reason: The earlier summary said the text 'names the elder'; Rashi's contrast is between the explicit 'her father' and the pronoun 'him'.

value: The speech changes person: the elder speaks of her completed act in the first singular (שָׁכַבְתִּי), then proposes in the first plural (נַשְׁקֶנּוּ, וּנְחַיֶּה), and gives the younger her part in the second feminine singular (וּבֹאִי, שִׁכְבִי).

נַשְׁקֶנּוּ is the hifil cohortative with the suffix 'him' joined by a doubled nun (an energic ending): 'let us make him drink'. The clause repeats the act of 19:33 for the next night: 'also tonight' is the English of גַּם הַלַּיְלָה.
The reported act of the elder is in the qatal, and she gives its time as אֶמֶשׁ, the night just past.
The speech ends with the same clause as the elder's proposal in 19:32 (וּנְחַיֶּה מֵאָבִינוּ זָרַע), now spoken to the younger as the reason for the second night.
patches.reason: The last note said the two proposals were 'the elder's' and 'the younger's'; both are the elder's words, in 19:32 and here.
the entry lists senses of הוּא and this is the article-bearing 'that' (הַהוּא); no sense was given

patches.value: Infinitive construct with ו and ב: 'and in her rising'. Here the word is written without the ו after the ק (קֻמָהּ, with qibbuts); in 19:33 it is קוּמָהּ with the extra dots. Radak: it is written defectively, without a vav. The verb is the same.
patches.reason: The old note said 'the vowels differ' and missed the defective spelling that Radak remarks on

value: The verse repeats the frame of 19:33 with these changes: the subject (the younger), the verb of motion (וַתָּקׇם 'arose' for וַתָּבֹא 'came in'), the preposition (עִם for אֵת), the adverb גַּם 'also', the fuller הַהוּא 'that' (19:33 has הוּא), and the defective spelling בְּקֻמָהּ.

In both nights it is the daughters (plural) who make the father drink (19:33, 19:35); only the act of lying with him is done by one daughter each night, the elder first and then the younger. The father's ignorance is the same in both.
The adverb גַּם ties the second night to the first, as the speech in 19:34 had done.
patches.reason: The old note said the elder's act was 'she made drink' and the younger's 'she arose and lay'; both nights the daughters (plural) make him drink.

value: The verb is a wayyiqtol of הָרָה in the feminine plural, with the two daughters as subject; the English 'became pregnant' is the sense of the verb's Qal 1 entry.
The construct phrase שְׁתֵּי בְנוֹת־לוֹט is 'the two daughters of Lot': a construct chain ending in a proper name is definite, so the whole phrase has the sense of the article.
The verse gives the conception without a separate night for each daughter: the reader is left to place it.
patches.reason: the old note said 'no article is needed' and so gave 'two daughters'; the construct with Lot is definite

patches.value: Rashi: although a woman does not conceive from a first act of intercourse, these two took control of themselves and put their nakedness (their private parts) outward, and so conceived from the first act. The English does not adopt this physiological explanation; it is kept here because a reader may ask how both conceived after one night each.
patches.reason: 'thrown off restraint' reverses Rashi's שָׁלְטוּ בְעַצְמָן, 'they mastered themselves'

value.summary: Radak: they conceived from that one act, which shows that they did not lie with him again, for their only aim was to leave seed. The English 'became pregnant', set after each daughter's one night, agrees.

patches.reason: the meaning and the commentators' readings belong in the note

value.summary: Ibn Ezra gives two readings of עַד הַיּוֹם: that no foreign nation mixed with them (the Moabites) up to now, or that the matter is known to this day. The English renders the words 'to this day' and decides neither reading; both are kept here.

patches.reason: the English is neutral between his two readings; the old summary said it 'adopts the first', which it does not

value: Moab was a people of the plateau east of the Dead Sea, a neighbour of Israel in the Transjordan. Deuteronomy 2:9 says that the LORD gave Ar to the descendants of Lot as a possession.
Moab is known also from outside the Bible: it is a kingdom in the Mesha stele, a royal inscription of Moab from the ninth century BCE.

The text gives Moab and Ammon an origin: both descend from Lot through his daughters, after the destruction of the cities (19:24-29). It states only the descent; whether the account preserves a tradition of kinship with these peoples or expresses Israel's view of them is discussed.

The name is explained by sound, as many names in Genesis are: 'Moab' is joined to מֵאָב, 'from a father'. Such explanations are the narrator's wordplay and are not necessarily the name's linguistic origin.
patches.reason: adds the extra-biblical attestation, the debated sense of the genealogy and the nature of the name-explanation

patches.value: The name בֶּן־עַמִּי is a transliteration: 'son of my people' (the lexicon's gloss), or in Radak's words 'from my family'. It sounds like בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן, 'sons of Ammon', and the text links the two by sound. The English keeps the name, as the decisions require.
patches.reason: the old note attributed 'son of my people' to Radak; he says 'from my family' (מִמִּשְׁפַּחְתִּי); the link of sound to Ammon is the point of the explanation

value: The pronoun is written הוא and read הִיא (the Torah's regular ketiv/qere for the feminine pronoun); the pointing הִוא is the qere. The English follows the reading: 'she'.
patches.reason: the decisions require the ketiv to be recorded in the apparatus

patches.value: Radak: the name בֶּן־עַמִּי means 'from my family I had this son'. And this daughter was more modest than the firstborn, for she did not reveal that he was from her father (שֶׁלֹּא גִּלְּתָה מִן אָבִיהָ).
patches.reason: the old summary said she did not disclose the matter to her father; Radak says she did not make plain that the son was from her father

value: Ammon was a people of the Transjordan, north-east of Moab and east of the Jordan, with its centre at Rabbah (later Amman). Deuteronomy 2:19 gives the land of the sons of Ammon to the descendants of Lot.
The name בֶּן־עַמִּי, 'son of my people', resembles בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן, 'sons of Ammon': as with Moab, the text joins the name of the people to the name of the child by sound.
patches.reason: adds the sound-link that the explanation rests on
